title: "Why business education matters for scientists"

## From research to business impact

My career started in scientific research: a PhD at the University of Tübingen,
postdoctoral work at ETH Zürich on efficient soil sensing, and years of developing
machine-learning methods for spectroscopy and environmental applications.

At BUCHI Labortechnik, my role moved towards driving innovation and digital
transformation in a company that builds analytical instruments. That shift made one
thing clear to me: research has real value only when it informs meaningful,
data-driven decisions, and turning a good model into a product or a service is as
much an organisational problem as a technical one. To address that gap, I completed
a part-time MSc in Business Analytics at Imperial College London.

## Why a master's after a PhD

I was often asked this question. A PhD shows you how much there is still to learn,
and continuous learning is part of how scientists work. I wanted structured knowledge
in business analytics, decision-making and strategy: the skills that turn technical
work into implemented solutions rather than prototypes.

## What changed in how I work

**Implementation over invention.** The programme shifted my focus from building
solutions to making them work inside organisations: aligning technical work with
business needs, balancing trade-offs, and managing knowledge across teams.

**Communication as a project tool.** The modules on leadership, negotiation and
communication showed how much clear communication matters at every level.
Managing conflict well is not about keeping the peace; it keeps projects on track
and avoids costly delays.

**Transferable expertise.** Specialists tend to stay within narrow fields. I learned
to look for problems in other areas where my expertise can make a difference, which
has broadened the scope of what I contribute across disciplines.

## Scaling impact beyond the lab

For several years I have worked with the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization
(FAO) on optical spectroscopy as a faster, cheaper and more sustainable alternative
to conventional soil testing, with a focus on making these tools accessible in low-
and middle-income countries. This includes training materials for scientists,
technicians and students worldwide. The business perspective strengthened how I
approach this work: project management, communication with diverse stakeholders,
and scaling training efforts.

## For scientists considering the same step

A scientific background is a real asset in business education. Analytical thinking,
a structured approach and clear communication transfer directly. If you care about
science and want your work to have impact beyond your field, learning the language
of strategy and decision-making is one of the most effective investments you can
make.
